Moving from highly controlled laboratory conditions to manufacturing reality nearly always requires additional degrees of approximation, extrapolation and assumption due to the further expanding set of interacting variables. The reality of manufacturing requires simultaneous management of purity (S. D. Imhoff et al. 2019), thermo-mechanical processing history (Bostrom et al. 1955), and ultimately the performance during irradiation (Bleiberg, Jones, and Lustman 1956; Bleiberg 1959). It is advantageous therefore to link variables to behavior through material models and data in order to find an optimal mixture of expedient, impactful, and economical areas of research. U-Mo is useful as an alloy system, in part, because of the large solubility range of Mo in U combined with the ability to retain the high temperature BCC phase upon quenching; making the material behavior somewhat predictable. Considering that one common route for U-Mo alloy manufacture is by casting, the details of the liquid to solid transition are very important. Process parameters, especially as defined during early development of new products, often require information contained in available phase diagrams. For instance, a common first challenge to reliably achieve sound castings with new alloys can be overcome by understanding freezing range characteristics. Additionally, the ultimate time and temperature for chemical homogenization is is dependent upon the amplitude of microsegregation and the dendrite spacing within the solidified metal. Finally, robust designs for molds and process parameters require detailed inputs such as the enthalpy release characteristics during solidification and any subsequent phase transformations experienced during cooling. In essence, the structures and properties that are important for downstream processing and for ultimate performance of the materials in service are initialized during solidification. The goal in writing this report is primarily to provide information to practitioners regarding the liquidus, solidus, and heat of fusion for alloys in the U-rich region of the U-Mo binary system. The overall approach is to make measurements which fill significant gaps in the existing data so that current constructions of the phase relationships may be used with more confidence or at least with a firm understanding of the uncertainty. Differential thermal analysis (DTA) is the primary means by which these measurements have been made; with supporting metallography, laser flash analysis (LFA), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) measurements.
